A.explanation: Too small by a factor of $10^4$ because the $\mu\text{A}$ to $\text{A}$ and $\text{mV}$ to $\text{V}$ conversions were not applied correctly.

B.explanation: Too small by a factor of $10^3$ from confusing $\text{pJ}$ with $\text{nJ}$ when converting $1.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ J}$.

C.explanation: Too small by a factor of 10, giving $1.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ J}$ instead of the correct $1.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ J}$ product of $VIt$.

hints: Start by listing what is given: $I = 0.10 \, \mu\text{A}$, $V = 10 \, \text{mV}$ and $t = 10 \, \text{s}$, so first convert micro to $10^{-6}$ and milli to $10^{-3}$.
Connect current and potential difference to power with $P = VI$, which gives the energy transfer rate in watts.
Multiply that power by the $10 \, \text{s}$ time using $E = Pt = VIt$, then convert $10^{-8} \, \text{J}$ to $\text{nJ}$ using $1 \, \text{nJ} = 10^{-9} \, \text{J}$.
walkthrough: Identify the useful values: $I = 0.10 \, \mu\text{A}$, $V = 10 \, \text{mV}$ and time $t = 10 \, \text{s}$ for energy dissipated.
State the electrical power rule: $P = VI$, so $P = (1.0 \times 10^{-2}) \times (1.0 \times 10^{-7}) = 1.0 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{W}$.
Calculate dissipated energy with $E = Pt = VIt$: $E = (1.0 \times 10^{-9}) \times 10 = 1.0 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{J}$.
Convert joules to nanojoules: $1.0 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{J} = 10 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{J} = 10 \, \text{nJ}$. This is option D.
